title: Chapter X

teacherSummary.text: Miss Bingley flatters Darcy as he writes a letter; Elizabeth and Darcy spar over Bingley's 'humility' and persuadability. Darcy asks Elizabeth to dance a reel; she refuses wittily, and he finds himself 'bewitched.'

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter X,” how does Austen show wit as courtship? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter X develops the idea of wit as courtship. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter X to complicate the reader's understanding of wit as courtship. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter X within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of wit as courtship responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter X as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of wit as courtship. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: “I dare say you believed it; but I am by no means convinced that you would be gone with such celerity. Your conduct would be quite as dependant on chance as that of any man I know; and if, as you were mounting your horse, a friend were to say, ‘Bingley, you had better stay till next week,’ you would probably do it, you would probably not go—and, at another word, might stay a month.”

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Why does Darcy enjoy Elizabeth's refusal rather than resent it? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include appertain, overthrowing, celerity, rambled, premeditated. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: ““Will it not be advisable, before we proceed on this subject, to arrange with rather more precision the degree of importance which is to appertain to this request, as well as the degree of intimacy subsisting between the parties?”” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To belong or pertain, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Letter writing was a central social skill and a sign of character. Now, why does this chapter matter? Their verbal duels reveal mutual attraction neither admits. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Theme.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: “I dare say you believed it; but I am by no means convinced that you would be gone with such celerity.
